title: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)
summary: Describes Classless Inter-Domain Routing, which allocates IP addresses in flexible blocks instead of fixed classes. This helps conserve the address space and slow the growth of routing tables. It was replaced by RFC 4632.

plainLanguage.summary: Before CIDR, IP addresses came in three fixed sizes and the Internet was running out of the middle one. This RFC proposes handing out addresses in large blocks instead, so that a router in another part of the network needs one entry to cover thousands of addresses rather than one entry per small network. It also sets out two rules that make the summarisation safe.

subtitle: The plan that stopped IPv4 addresses being handed out one class at a time.

tldr.problem: IP addresses were handed out in fixed classes, so a site needing 300 hosts had to take a block that could hold 65,000, and every routing table in the Internet had to carry an entry for every one of those small networks.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of individual class C networks, service providers are given large blocks that fall on bit boundaries, and they sub-allocate from those. Routers then advertise one route covering a whole block, and forwarding picks the most specific matching route.
tldr.outcome: Routing tables stop growing at the previous rate and the class B space stops running out. The document was a Proposed Standard and has been replaced by RFC 4632.

today: RFC 1519 was published in September 1993 as a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4632, which restates the classless addressing and routing strategy. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1338.

sections.title: The Problems This Was Written to Solve
sections.content:
As the Internet grew it became clear that it was about to face several serious scaling problems. The first was exhaustion of the class B network address space, whose fundamental cause was the lack of a class of a size suited to a mid-sized organisation: class C, with a maximum of 254 host addresses, was too small, while class B, which allows up to 65534 addresses, was too large for most organisations. The second was growth of routing tables in Internet routers beyond the ability of current software, hardware and people to manage. The third was eventual exhaustion of the 32-bit address space.

The RFC states that the first two were likely to become critical within the next one to three years. It does not try to solve the third, which is a longer-term problem, but tries to ease enough of the short to mid-term difficulty for the Internet to keep working while progress is made on a longer-term solution. The plan is meant to be viable for at least three years.

The proposed solution is to allocate future address space topologically, by allocating segments of the address space to transit routing domains. The plan neither requires nor assumes that already assigned addresses will be reassigned, though doing so would further reduce routing table sizes. It also does not require a domain to renumber if it changes its service provider, though domains are encouraged to renumber so that their individual address allocations do not have to be advertised one by one.
sections.plainLanguage: Two problems were pressing. There were not enough class B networks left, because a site needing a few hundred addresses had to take a block that could hold tens of thousands. And routing tables everywhere were growing faster than the equipment could keep up. The third problem, running out of addresses altogether, is left for a later plan.

sections.title: Allocating Address Space in Blocks
sections.content:
The plan has two components: distributing the allocation of address space, and providing a mechanism for aggregating routing information. The goal is to allocate address space so that routing information can be aggregated along topological lines. For simple, single-homed clients, allocating their address space out of a transit routing domain's space does this automatically: rather than advertise a separate route for each client, the transit domain advertises a single aggregate route describing all the destinations connected to it.

The basic idea is to allocate one or more blocks of class C network numbers to each network service provider, and then to hand out bitmask-oriented subsets of a provider's space to the organisations using that provider. Hierarchical allocation of this kind means that, for routing purposes, a client with addresses from a given provider is part of that provider and is routed through its infrastructure, so routing information about multi-homed organisations still has to be known at higher levels of the hierarchy. The RFC argues that it is easier for a small number of service providers to obtain addresses from the central authority than for a much larger and constantly growing number of individual clients, and recommends that most, if not all, network numbers be distributed through service providers.

Two situations cost aggregation efficiency. Multi-homed organisations, connected to more than one provider, must be advertised into the system by each of their providers, so their routing information often cannot be aggregated into any one provider's space; their routing cost stays about the same as it is today. Organisations that change service provider without renumbering punch a hole in the original provider's aggregation; the plan handles this by requiring the newer provider to advertise a specific route for the client, which is preferred because it is the longest match, and by recommending that such organisations eventually migrate their address assignments into the new provider's space.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses are handed to service providers in big blocks, and providers hand slices of their block to their customers. A provider then needs one route to cover the whole block instead of one route per customer. Two cases break this: a customer connected to two providers at once, and a customer that moves to another provider but keeps its old addresses.

sections.title: The Case for Changing
sections.content:
An informal analysis of the network-contacts file as of 2/25/92 showed 46 of 126 class A network numbers allocated, leaving 81, and 5467 of 16382 class B numbers allocated, leaving 10915. Assuming recent trends continued, the number of allocated class B networks would double about once a year, and all class B networks would be exhausted within about 15 months. As of 1/13/93, 52 class A network numbers and 7133 class B networks had been allocated, and the RFC suggests the change in the class B allocation rate is due to the initial deployment of this plan.

The routing table figures are given month by month. In December 1988 the total number of routes advertised was 897; by December 1990 it was 2190; and by December 1992 it was 8561. A default-free routing table, such as those maintained by the NSFNET backbone routers, contained approximately 4700 entries as of January 1992, and the historic data showed this number doubling on average every 10 months between 1988 and 1991. On that rate the RFC expected a default-free table to reach approximately 30000 entries in two years.

Under the proposed plan the growth is greatly reduced, because most new address assignments come from one of the large blocks given to service providers. Assuming prompt implementation, that each provider's initial block satisfies its needs for two years, about 100 service providers, and that the number of multi-homed organisations doubles each year from fewer than 100 today, the total comes to 4700 + 800 + 150 = 5650, an annual growth rate of approximately 6 percent. The RFC contrasts this with the current annual growth of 130 percent. It notes that these are not conservative assumptions, and that with only 90 percent participation by service providers, the table would be 13145 routes at the end of three years, against roughly 75000 routes without any action.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does the arithmetic on the growth in routing tables and in address use, then runs it again with the plan in place. The projected growth rate drops from about 130 percent a year to about 6 percent, and the class B networks that were about to run out stop running out.

sections.title: Two Rules for Advertising Routes
sections.content:
Two semantic changes have to be made to inter-domain routing protocols. First, the concept of network class must be deprecated: routing destinations are represented as network and mask pairs, and routing is done on a longest-match basis, meaning that when a destination matches several network and mask pairs the match with the longest mask is used. Second, inter-domain protocols must support route aggregation, which they generally do not, so a new set of protocols is needed.

Rule one is that routing to all destinations must be done on a longest-match basis only. This means that destinations which are multi-homed relative to a routing domain must always be explicitly announced into that domain, because they cannot be summarised: if a network is multi-homed, all of its paths into a routing domain higher in the hierarchy must be known to that higher network.

Rule two is that a routing domain which summarises multiple routes must discard packets which match the summarisation but do not match any of the explicit routes making it up. This is necessary to prevent routing loops in the presence of less specific information such as a default route. One implementation is for the border router to keep a sink route for each of its aggregations, so that by longest match all traffic for components of the aggregation that are not explicitly known is discarded.

The RFC then works through why rule two matters. A mid-level network holding 2048 class C networks starting at 192.24.0.0 advertises 192.24.0.0/255.248.0.0 to a backbone that holds 192.0.0.0/255.0.0.0. If the mid-level loses internal connectivity to 192.24.1.0, traffic from the backbone follows the mid-level's advertised route, and on arrival the mid-level must not follow the 192.0.0.0/255.0.0.0 route it learned from the backbone, since that would loop. The default route is a special case of the same rule.

Beyond the rules, implementations should accept an arbitrary network number and mask for all routing destinations, with the constraint that the mask must be contiguous. The degenerate route 0.0.0.0 with mask 0.0.0.0 is the default route and must be accepted by all implementations, but should never be advertised unless specific configuration says so. The domain allocated a range of addresses has the sole authority over aggregating its own space, usually through manual configuration on its border routers, and may delegate that authority to another domain. Preconfiguration of the ranges to aggregate is recommended over working it out purely from dynamically learned routes, because a route that is missing cannot always be distinguished from one that is temporarily unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules make the summarisation safe. Routing always uses the most specific matching route, so a site with two providers has to be announced explicitly by both. And a router that advertises a summary must drop any packet for an address inside that summary that it does not know about, rather than sending it back out through the summary it learned from further away.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The example allocates a block of 2048 class C network numbers beginning with 192.24.0.0 and ending with 192.31.255.0 to a single provider, RA. A supernetted route to that block is described as 192.24.0.0 with mask 255.248.0.0. RA connects six clients, each of which is given a contiguous power-of-two block: C1 gets 192.24.0 through 192.24.7, described by the route 192.24.0.0 with mask 255.255.248.0; C2 gets 192.24.16 through 192.24.31, with route 192.24.16.0 and mask 255.255.240.0; C3 gets 192.24.8 through 192.24.11, with mask 255.255.252.0; C4 gets 192.24.12 through 192.24.15, with mask 255.255.252.0; C5 gets 192.24.32 and 192.24.33, with mask 255.255.254.0; and C6 gets 192.24.34 and 192.24.35, with mask 255.255.254.0. If RA uses an interior protocol that supports classless networks it can perform the supernetting where it connects to its clients and keep only six distinct routes for the 36 class C networks; otherwise explicit routes to all 36 must be carried by the interior protocol.

To make the example realistic, C4 and C5 are multi-homed through another provider, RB, and a client C7 that originally used RB has moved to RA and keeps a block allocated out of RB's space, 192.32.0 through 192.32.15, described by 192.32.0.0 with mask 255.255.240.0. C4 is primary through RA and secondary through RB; C5 is primary through RB and secondary through RA. The two providers are joined by a backbone provider, BB.

Following rule one, RA advertises to BB the block it was given and C7, and also C4 because C4 is multi-homed with RA as primary. C5 need not be advertised, since longest match at BB will pick RB as primary and RA's aggregate serves as the secondary. RA's advertisements are 192.24.12.0/255.255.252.0 as primary for C4, 192.32.0.0/255.255.240.0 as primary for C7, and 192.24.0.0/255.248.0.0 as primary for the remainder of RA. RB must advertise C4 and C5 as well as its own block, and may advertise that C7 is unreachable: 192.24.12.0/255.255.252.0 secondary, 192.24.32.0/255.255.254.0 primary, and 192.32.0.0/255.248.0.0 primary.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example gives one provider a block of 2048 small networks and shows how it hands out pieces of it, each piece sized to the customer and each described by a single address and mask. Two customers are connected to a second provider as well, and the example shows exactly which routes each provider advertises to the backbone that connects them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section of the memo is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The rest of the document does contain rules that matter for correctness rather than for defence. Rule two is the clearest example: a router that advertises a summary must discard packets for addresses inside that summary that it does not know about. Without that rule, a packet for a destination that has become unreachable could be sent to the router that summarised it, and back out again along the summary it learned from further away, forming a loop between two routers instead of being dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says nothing about security. What it does insist on is that a router drops traffic it cannot account for rather than passing it on, because passing it on is what turns a broken route into a loop between two routers.

viz.caption: HOW ONE PROVIDER SPLITS ITS BLOCK AMONG CUSTOMERS

items.title: Longest match only
items.text: When several routes match a destination, the one with the longest mask is used, so a multi-homed site must be announced explicitly.

items.title: Discard the unknown
items.text: A router that advertises a summary must drop packets for addresses inside that summary that no explicit route covers.

items.title: Contiguous masks
items.text: Any network number and mask may be used for a destination, but the mask must be contiguous.

items.title: Default route accepted
items.text: The route 0.0.0.0 with mask 0.0.0.0 must be accepted by every implementation, but not advertised without explicit configuration.

items.title: Configured aggregation ranges
items.text: The domain holding a block decides what to summarise, and preconfiguring the ranges is recommended over inferring them from live routes.
